report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans is **unproven**. While capsaicin exhibits anti-cancer activity in laboratory experiments, no clinical trials demonstrate that it treats or cures breast cancer in human patients.

### Summary of Evidence

1. **Preclinical Research (*In Vitro* and Animal Studies):** 
In cell culture and animal models, capsaicin inhibits cell proliferation and triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death) in human breast cancer cells by regulating signaling pathways such as EGFR/HER-2 and NF-κB (https://www.nature.com/articles/onc2009335, https://www.dovepress.com/capsaicin-inhibits-proliferation-and-induces-apoptosis-in-breast-cance-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT).

2. **Lack of Human Clinical Proof:** 
Laboratory success does not translate directly to human cancer treatment. Using capsaicin as an anti-cancer drug in humans remains speculative due to low bioavailability, difficulty reaching target tumor sites in effective concentrations, and potential side effects (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/, https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/).

3. **Current Human Clinical Applications:** 
In human clinical medicine, capsaicin patches are studied and used primarily to manage localized neuropathic pain resulting from cancer surgeries or chemotherapy, not to shrink or treat cancer tumors directly.
